speaker-d2-ai-studio-1510.titel: Innovation scales on trust: what central banking can teach us about scaling AI
speaker-d2-ai-studio-1510.speaker: Nino Landerer (Deutsche Bundesbank)
speaker-d2-ai-studio-1510.transkript:
Good afternoon.
I hope you got some coffee.
I saw there were some long lines for the coffee, but I hope you got-
We're kicking off the afternoon with an institution that is on first sight not-
For experiments, the German Central Bank.
And that's exactly why it's made worth a look to hear and to learn from the Deputy Director General Strategy.
Nino Landerer, welcome on stage.
Thank you so much.
Now I'll present you the problem that probably happens to almost everyone in this room today.
You pay for a coffee, a train ticket, perhaps a taxi.
Your taxi card opens an app or press the button, and then you move on.
You probably didn't pause, but you wonder whether the payments would go through.
Whether the recipient would receive the money.
Or whether the bank at the other end would still be there tomorrow.
That confidence is not automatic.
It is built.
It rests on institutions, rules, technology, supervision, and habits of-
Trust.
...
accumulated over decades.
Most of the time, we do not see this machinery.
And that is precisely the point.
The best critical infrastructure is almost invisible when it works.
We notice electricity when the lights go out.
We notice payments when the terminal says, "Declined."
Central banks are part of the architecture that makes money and payments dependable.
We do not do this alone, obviously.
The central banking perspective begins with a very simple question.
What has to keep working even under pressure?
AI is approaching a similar moment.
As we speak, AI is moving up the adoption ladder.
But the road from impressive technology to trusted infrastructure is still a long one.
We will only fully rely on AI in the most important parts of our economy and everyday lives if it becomes-
...
reliable, accountable, and trustworthy.
And that is why I believe central banking has something useful to say about AI.
That leads me to my thesis for today: Innovation scales on trust.
In other words, capability gets attention.
Trust gets adoption.
Central banks do not have all the answers about AI, and we certainly do not.
But we have experience in thinking about-
...
powerful innovations from at least three perspectives.
First, as economists.
What might AI mean for growth, productivity,
and inflation?
Second, as guardians of resilience.
What could go wrong when a technology becomes fast, concentrated, and deeply embedded?
Answer it as users.
What does it take to deploy these tools reliably inside complex institutions?
More accuracy.
Accountability and public confidence matter a lot.
Let me take those three perspectives in turn and close with a brief outlook.
The first perspective is the obvious one.
What will AI do to the economy?
In 1987, the economist Robert Solow made his famous observation.
You can see the computer age everywhere in the productivity statistics.
At the time, computers were already transforming offices, factories, and homes.
Yet, the promised economy-wide productivity surge was difficult to find in the data.
In the United States, strong productivity growth became more visibly only in the mid to late 1990s.
Electricity is an even older example.
Factories were electrified from the 1880s, but as a historian Paul David showed, the big
gains came in the 1920s.
Owners first swapped a steam engine for an electric motor and kept the same layout.
The gains arrived when they redesigned the factory floor around the new power source.
The lessons are important.
AI has the potential to become a major force in the global economy.
Its eventual impact could be substantial.
But scale, timing, and distribution remain uncertain as of yet.
And there is a large difference between using AI somewhere in an organization and reorganizing an organization-
...
especially obviously on a macroeconomic scale.
The first is an experiment, the second is a-
Transformation.
And transformations do take time.
Consumer and employee use of AI tools may be spreading exceptionally quickly.
They do.
But rapid access is not the same as economy-wide transformation.
The harder task is embedding AI reliably in business processes, redesigning organizations and-
For central banks, this creates a genuine challenge.
Monetary policy must respond to the economy we have, not merely the economy promised in investor presentations.
In the short run, AI can increase demand.
Building the infrastructure requires substantial investment.
Data centers, semiconductors, power generation.
Those investments create activity now.
The productivity gains, however, may come later.
If demand rises before the economy's capacity rises with it, the near-term effect can be inflationary.
This depends on many things, obviously.
How investment is financed, the availability of labor and energy.
The extent to which equipment is imported and the broader state of the economy.
But the basic sequencing is worth remembering.
Investment now, gains later.
AI could lower costs and expand productive capacity over time.
But the route there may be inflationary if investments, electricity demand, and expectations for
price before the productivity gains are realized.
If AI eventually enables firms to produce more with the same labor and capital, it could raise potential growth.
And ease price pressures over time.
That's what you hear, what the promise is.
It could also affect investment opportunities.
And eventually the interest rate consistent with stable inflation.
But we should be careful.
Higher productivity does not automatically translate into higher economy-wide growth.
It depends on whether innovations spread beyond a handful of frontier firms where the more
.
And whether the new capacity can be built quickly enough.
That uncertainty is not a reason for complacency.
It is a reason for humility.
We need to ask, where is AI being deployed?
Is it changing business processes?
Is it increasing output?
Is it creating new bottlenecks in power, skills, or infrastructure?
I would say yes to many of these questions.
And is it changing the balance between demand today and supply tomorrow?
I think that's one of the key questions.
These are not glamorous questions, obviously, but they determine whether an innovation becomes a macroeconomic trend.
Transformation or simply an expensive set of tools.
The second perspective I would like to touch upon is about resilience.
Financial systems are built on trust.
Trust is not sentiment alone.
It is a practical expectation that systems will function when they are needed.
Including on difficult days.
History offers several useful warnings about automation and digital dependency.
The first one is speed.
On May 6th, 2010, US equity markets experienced what became known as the Flash Crash.
The Dow Jones fell by almost 1,000 points, around 9% at the time, in a matter of minutes before-
Yeah.
...
the episode had many courses and no single women.
I will expose a fundamental mismatch.
Markets and machines could move at extraordinary speed, while human understanding and formal accountability-
The official investigation of this event took months.
The lesson of this is not that false systems are bad.
Modern finance, logistics, and communications, and much more depend on this speed.
The essence is when systems can act in milliseconds, controls need to be designed for milliseconds too.
It has to be embedded in limits, alerts, circuit breakers, escalation paths, and the ability to-
The second warning, apart from speed, is concentration.
In July 2024, a defective software update from a single cybersecurity provider caused disruption
across an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices, according to Microsoft.
Airlines, hospitals-
...
banks, broadcasters, and public services were affected.
It was not a cyberattack.
It was an operational failure in a widely used component of digital infrastructure.
AI has its own concentration risks.
Advanced chips, chip manufacturing, cloud infrastruc-
...
from tier model development, model hosting and distribution are concentrated in different ways.
The broad point is clear.
A growing number of organizations are relying on a relatively small number of companies-
...
to politics adds to the complexity here.
This can bring economies of scale and rapid innovation, this concentration, but it can also create common points of-
And the third warning...
Is deception.
Earlier in 2024, Hong Kong police reported a case in which a finance employee was persuaded to transfer around 20-
...
5 million US dollars after joining a video call with what appeared to be senior colleagues.
Two individuals obviously on the call were, as investigators said, synthetic fakes.
For generations, seeing and hearing someone has been foundations of practical trust.
Now, seeing and hearing someone can obviously no longer be taken at face value.
If identity becomes synthetic, trust has to move from appearance to cryptographic procedural
and institutional proof.
These three cases, the flash crash, the software outage, and the synthetic impersonation, share a common message.
The problem was not that the technology was weak.
It was not.
The safeguards had not kept in pace-
...
with speed, concentration or realism.
For central banks, the objective is not to stop experimentation.
Innovation, productivity, and competition obviously matter.
But failure must be survivable.
For the system as a whole.
It is the end system.
It's not one that never makes mistake.
It is one in which mistakes can be detected.
Contained and prevented from becoming a system-wide crisis.
The third perspective is more practical.
Central banks are, among other things, large information processors.
We analyze economic data, financial market development, supervisory information, et cetera.
Many central banks have used machine learning tools productively in analytical and operational work for years.
They are now building on that experience, assess and deploy language technologies.
The experience is useful because it shifts attention from the model itself.
To the system around it.
Therefore, the first lesson here is that the model is rarely the whole system.
A powerful model can still produce poor outcome if it is fed incomplete data, placed-
...
in a weak workflow, given an ambiguous task, or used by people who do not understand its limitations.
In practice, the surrounding system often matters more than the headline model.
Data quality, access controls, documentation, testing, monitoring, and clear ownership of decisions.
The second lesson is validation.
Start by validating models on tasks where we know the answer.
Before using AI in a consequential process, evaluate it-
...
compare its output with reliable benchmarks.
Looking not only at average performance, but at edge cases, too.
Fail modes and the errors that the human review may miss.
And the third lesson concerns human oversight.
Human in the loop has become a reassuring phrase, but it can conceal more than it reveals.
Human oversight is meaningful only if the persons involved have the time and-
...
and authority to actually challenge the system.
If a revenue is asked to approve hundreds of AI-generated outputs under time pressure without access to the underlying-
...
evidence and without the ability to stop the process, then the person is not really in the loop.
They're simply providing a signature at the end.
That is not oversight, it is theater.
And in consequential settings, it is dangerous.
It creates the appearance of human control without the capacity-
Trustworthy AI therefore cannot be added at the end after the product has been built and sold.
It-
It has to be designed in from the beginning through the system integration and appropriate validation guided by-
That is also the purpose of the Bundesbank's AI strategy.
To make AI, to make artificial intelligence an integral part of the Bundesbank's toolkit, which we use-
To fulfill our statutory tasks.
Safety, responsibility, and human accountability remain clear.
Let me close with a brief outlook.
We should be modest about forecasting AI.
The history of technology is full of premature certainty, predictions of effortless abundance.
We hear that-
...
many times.
Predictions of inevitable collapse, that's the other part, and predictions that the future-
...
will be live on a specific timetable.
So, scenarios can help us think more clearly.
Consider two questions.
The first one is about technology.
Does AI keep accelerating or does progress slow?
And the second one is about money.
Does investment keep flowing or does it dry up?
Put the two questions together and you get a two-by-two table with four different futures.
First, your business case, acceleration with sustained investment.
Progress compounds and capital keeps flowing.
I would say that's where we are now, more or less.
AI systems move from assisting people to acting for them.
Transacting with each other at machine speed.
Productivity finally shows up in the statistics.
I would say we're not there yet.
This is an optimistic case, but not a painless one.
Investment arrives still before the game.
So inflation pressure comes first and labor markets shift faster than retraining can follow.
Second is slow progress, slow technological progress, but with sustained investment.
This is the fragile quadrant.
Capital fleet keeps flowing in on expectations the technology has not yet met.
That rises and some funding turns circular.
With a supplier's financing to customers who buy their products.
I think this is something many of us have also maybe seen in the news.
It's a blast.
Either technology catches up or the money runs out.
The third quadrant is technology succeeds, but the money dries up.
And this is the most instructive one.
When the dot-com boom ended in 2000, the NASDAQ lost about three quarters of its value.
Yet the internet was obviously not a failure.
The fiber network during the excess in the 1990s carried the next generation of the network
devices that made new businesses possible.
Technology can succeed so well that it makes capacity cheap, and cheap capacity destroys the returns of those-
Wonderful for users, brutal for owners of expensive assets.
The policy task is to-
Stop the financial damage from destroying the lasting value.
